headline: East end ebb at 5:40: bass hold the rip, blues crash bait through
subhead: The moon's building fast now and the current's sharpening right on schedule — here's where the Canal is paying off and where it's still a grind.
body_markdown:
The east tide started running hard out of Cape Cod Bay around 5:40 this past week, and that's the number that's mattered most. Not the moon, not the wind — the clock on the current. Thirty years watching this ditch and the lesson never changes: the Canal doesn't care what the calendar says, it cares what the water's doing between the Bourne and Sagamore bridges, and right now that water is moving with more push than it had two weeks ago. We flagged that last week — said the building moon would tighten current strength and sharpen the bite windows — and that's exactly what's happened. Full moon is coming up fast, and every tide between now and then is going to run a little harder, a little longer, and the fish know it before we do.

The pattern this week has been current-driven striper fishing, plain and simple. Bass are stacked on the seams where the fast water meets the slower water — the classic rip lines off the Railroad Bridge and down through the Sagamore side toward the power lines. These aren't blitzing fish jumping all over bait balls; this is a working bite, fish holding in the current and eating what gets swept past them. Swimming plugs — Red Fins and Danny-style plugs in bone and mackerel patterns — worked on the outgoing east tide have been the most consistent producers, especially in that last two hours of flow when the current really starts ripping and bait gets pinned against the rocks. Bucktails in white and chartreuse, 1.5 to 2 ounces depending on how hard it's running, dragged slow along bottom on the drop-off edges, have picked up fish in the 28 to 34-inch range mixed with shorts. Nobody's filling a cooler with overslots down here — this is a keeper-slot mixed bag, honest work for honest effort, not a blitz.

Bluefish have been the more reliable player of the two species this week, and that tracks with what we've been saying — bluefish activity follows bunker density, and there's enough peanut bunker and adult bunker pushing through both ends of the Canal right now to keep the blues committed. They're crashing bait on top during the stronger push of current, particularly at the west end near the Mashnee flats and around Hog Island, where the west-running tide funnels bait against the Buzzards Bay side structure. Poppers and metal — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters — thrown into visible surface activity have been the play there, and it's been good enough that a few boats working out of Phinneys Harbor have made it a short-run pattern: hit the west end on the building west tide, work the bird activity, and be done by mid-morning before the current slacks off and the bite goes quiet.

Fluke are still around but this is the softening part of the season for them, right on schedule. The deeper channel edges near the Mashnee Island cut and the holes off Wings Neck have been giving up keeper fluke to white Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails, worked slow on the last of the ebb when the current eases enough to fish it properly without getting swept sideways. It's not a numbers game anymore — one or two keepers for an hour of drifting is realistic — but the fish are there and they'll stay catchable on structure through September before they start sliding toward deeper water.

The piece everybody at the shop is talking about is what's happening east of here. False albacore have started showing in Nantucket Sound and on the Cape Cod Bay side, and bonito have already crashed hard into Block Island and Point Judith. That's the leading edge of a push that typically works its way along the coast, and the Canal's east end mouth off Scusset Beach is exactly the kind of current-swept structure that pulls albies in once they commit to this stretch. Nothing confirmed yet inside the Canal itself — the reports so far are fussy fish on tiny bait outside the rips — but if that pattern follows its usual track, the next week to two weeks is when Scusset and the east end jetty could turn into an albie spot worth the long cast with a Deadly Dick or small epoxy jig on light tackle.

Looking ahead: expect the current to keep building as the moon rounds toward full over the next several days, which means longer, harder-running tides at both ends and potentially shorter, more defined bite windows rather than long lazy grazing periods. If there's only one tide to fish this week, make it the east end on the tail of the east-flowing current — that two-hour window before slack has been the most consistent for stripers holding the rip. West end anglers should watch the west tide push past Mashnee and Hog Island early, before the Labor Day boat traffic picks up and pushes the bite around. The bunker are still building in the bay systems on both sides of the Canal, and once those schools tighten up further with the stronger moon tides, this stretch of water usually turns from a working bite into something with real teeth. Not there yet — but the pieces are lining up.
